where: Section 1 (passive and active attacks), exam trap 2, and Quiz Q5
problem: The chapter states flatly that 'A replay is fabrication' and keys the answer to Q5 to that. Its own definition of fabrication is 'a new message is inserted and made to look like it came from a real sender', which a replayed copy is not: the copy is old and the sender is genuine. Standard treatments do not agree here; replay is commonly placed under modification (an old message is substituted for the fresh one expected, so the stream is altered) and sometimes under fabrication (a copy is inserted). Presenting one choice as fact will cost students marks against an answer key that uses the other.
fix: Say: a replay is an active attack whose class is contested. Write 'modification of the message stream, sometimes listed as fabrication' and accept either in Q5's key. Keep the (correct) point that the copying is passive interception while the re-insertion is active.

where: Worked example 1, step 4 and the answer
problem: 'Attack class = fabrication/repudiation' contradicts the chapter's own line in Section 1, 'Every named attack is one of them', since repudiation is not one of the four classes. A sender who really sent the file and then denies it is not fabricating a message; X.800 treats repudiation as a separate threat against which the non-repudiation service is defined. The hybrid label also teaches a phrase that examiners do not accept as an attack class.
fix: Write: the event is not one of the four message classes; it is the threat of repudiation. The receiver cannot prove later that the sender sent the file, so the missing service is non-repudiation, met by a digital signature with a notarised timestamp. If a class must be given, note only that a false denial by a party is treated as fabrication by the receiving side; repudiation itself is a separate X.800 threat category.

problem: The event says the file body 'is unreadable', so confidentiality was not broken. The question then asks for 'one mechanism that would have prevented it', and the answer gives encipherment, which is already in place. A student will be unsure whether to name the mechanism already working or a further one.
fix: Ask 'which service was attacked, and what kept it safe?' Answer: interception of the contents failed because encipherment was already applied; the part still exposed is the pattern of who sent what to whom and when, which traffic padding and careful routing reduce.

problem: The lead says 'Attack classes, the X.800 service list and the X.800 mechanism list are the standard vocabulary for all three'. Only the service and mechanism lists come from X.800; the four attack classes come from the OSI-model attack taxonomy (interruption, interception, modification, fabrication) as presented in the standard security texts. A reader may wrongly cite X.800 for the four classes.
fix: Say: 'The service and mechanism lists come from X.800. The four attack classes come from the OSI attack taxonomy used in the standard security texts.'
